item.title: Timestral: Mistral's time-series foundation models
item.description:
Source: mistral.ai

Top Comment:

My field is primarily audio/vision ML so I don't have any particular domain expertise, but I don't get how you can lump all "time-series" together in one big bucket. My naive understanding is that the way to improve the accuracy is to gain as much joint information as possible. Like:

> Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.

To me this should be the entire basis of the system, not a condition to improve forecast quality? Like if you're modelling electricity consumption, if all you have is a window of N previous samples, you're going to get completely beaten by a comparatively simple system that knows the time of day, that there's holidays coming up, the weather forecast, etc.

I would also think that these time-series forecasting models would gain from a sophisticated understanding at least the labels of the covariates? A 5M model has no idea what a "bank holiday" is, it just sees an arbitrary class go from 0 to 1, and won't have any useful inductive biases as to what it means or how to link them to other pieces of information.

E.g., wouldn't you predict €/MWh of electricity far more accurately with access to price of natural gas (itself influenced by many geopolitical factors), breakdown in composition of production of each energy source, predictions about roll-out (requiring a sophisticated LLM capable of understanding news and their implications), etc. What's the use in trying to predict it from 2 variables and a narrow window looking back at just 8192 or 32768 samples?

Or perhaps I misunderstand the use-case and this is more for extremely short term movements?

item.title: If you don't run your own LLM proxy, how do you know whats going on?
item.description:
Source: jrdsgl.com

Top Comment:

You don't need a proxy to do this. I would argue you should not use a proxy to do this because the end result is a single point of failure direct in the line of your productivity.

Both Codex[0] and Claude Code[1] output OTEL traces that you can ingest and process.

Other harnesses like OpenCode, Pi, etc. you can hook into their plugin architecture and implement your own OTEL emission from a plugin (or use an off the shelf plugin[2]).

Host an OpenTelemetry collector[3][4] or rely on your existing collector infra (e.g. Datadog (no affiliation), AppInsights, etc.)

The OTEL traces will have exactly what you need. Tool calls, full prompts, token usage/cost, etc. It is less intrusive and does not become a single-point-of failure since the OTEL emission and collection is best-effort whereas a failing/overloaded proxy is going to strand your team until resolved. It's OK if you lose some OTEL traces; no productivity lost.

The configuration to enable this for Codex and CC is very straightforward (see [0][1] + [5])

--

[0] https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-advanced#o...

[1] https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage

[2] https://github.com/DEVtheOPS/opencode-plugin-otel

[3] Open source collector: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/

[4] Sample configuration for filtering noise: https://github.com/zeeq-ai/zeeq-app/blob/main/build/otel-col...

[5] Concrete examples of .codex/config.toml and .claude/settings.json: https://zeeq.ai/docs/key-features/session-telemetry#configur...

item.title: Let's Encrypt is adding two additional remote perspectives for domain validation
item.description:
Source: community.letsencrypt.org

Top Comment:

For anyone else who didn't have "remote perspectives" in their personal technical lexicon: this refers to performing the ACME challenge/response check when validating the domain of a certificate signing request from multiple physical locations, and therefore via multiple physical network routes, in order to make network-level attacks more difficult.

For example, if you were validating example.com, you'd need to set up some response to the ACME challenge somewhere, either through direct DNS-based validation (DNS-01, DNS-PERSIST-01) or through a server running at the resolved A/AAAA IP address for example.com (HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01). In all cases, when a CA goes to validate your challenge response, it relies both upon DNS and upon the network integrity between the CA's datacenters and your DNS and/or app servers. Both of these can be subverted, eg via BGP attack, to allow an attacker to replace a DNS response, re-route the destination IP address to a different server, etc, at which point they can inject their own challenge response, and therefore issue their own (unauthorized) certificates.

Multi-perspective validation means that the CA validates your challenge response from multiple datacenters on different networks instead of just one, such that a hypothetical network attack would have to target multiple independent networks in order to successfully issue their unauthorized certificate.

More info:

https://letsencrypt.org/2020/02/19/multi-perspective-validat...

https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/multi-perspective-valida...

I made it come up with a plan for this tool and had it implement the thing end to end in about 8 or 9 steps. It originally messed up the coordinate calculation but quickly corrected that when I pointed it out and other than that it one-shotted all the other steps.
